    <script>
        // ---------- bit helpers ----------
// bit = true = 1, false = 0, MSB first

function hexToBits(hex) {
     const bits = [];
    for (const ch of hex) {
        const n = parseInt(ch, 16);
        for (let i = 3; i >= 0; i--) bits.push(((n >> i) & 1) === 1);
    }
    return bits;
}

function bitsToHex(bits) {
    let hex = '';
    for (let i = 0; i < bits.length; i += 4) {
    let n = 0;
    for (let j = 0; j < 4; j++) n = (n << 1) | (bits[i + j] ? 1 : 0);
    hex += n.toString(16);
  }
  return hex;
}

function cloneBits(b) { return b.slice(); }

// ---------- 32-bit word ops, word = 32 booleans, MSB first ----------
function xorBits(a, b) { return a.map((v, i) => v !== b[i]); }
function andBits(a, b) { return a.map((v, i) => v && b[i]); }
function notBits(a) { return a.map(v => !v); }

function rotr(word, n) {
    // rotate right by n
    return word.slice(32 - n).concat(word.slice(0, 32 - n));
}

function shr(word, n) {
    // shift right, fill with false
    const out = new Array(32).fill(false);
    for (let i = 0; i < 32 - n; i++) out[i + n] = word[i];
    return out;
}

function addBits(...words) {
    // add any number of 32-bit words, mod 2^32
    let carry = 0;
    const out = new Array(32).fill(false);
    for (let i = 31; i >= 0; i--) {
        let sum = carry;
        for (const w of words) if (w[i]) sum++;
        out[i] = (sum % 2) === 1;
        carry = Math.floor(sum / 2);
    }
    return out;
}

// ---------- SHA-256 logical functions ----------
function Ch(x, y, z) {
     // (x AND y) XOR ((NOT x) AND z)
    return xorBits(andBits(x, y), andBits(notBits(x), z));
}
function Maj(x, y, z) {
    return xorBits(xorBits(andBits(x, y), andBits(x, z)), andBits(y, z));
}
function Sigma0(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 2), rotr(x, 13)), rotr(x, 22)); }
function Sigma1(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 6), rotr(x, 11)), rotr(x, 25)); }
function sigma0(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 7), rotr(x, 18)), shr(x, 3)); }
function sigma1(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 17), rotr(x, 19)), shr(x, 10)); }

// ---------- constants, as bits ----------
const K_HEX = [
 '428a2f98','71374491','b5c0fbcf','e9b5dba5','3956c25b','59f111f1','923f82a4','ab1c5ed5',
 'd807aa98','12835b01','243185be','550c7dc3','72be5d74','80deb1fe','9bdc06a7','c19bf174',
 'e49b69c1','efbe4786','0fc19dc6','240ca1cc','2de92c6f','4a7484aa','5cb0a9dc','76f988da',
 '983e5152','a831c66d','b00327c8','bf597fc7','c6e00bf3','d5a79147','06ca6351','14292967',
 '27b70a85','2e1b2138','4d2c6dfc','53380d13','650a7354','766a0abb','81c2c92e','92722c85',
 'a2bfe8a1','a81a664b','c24b8b70','c76c51a3','d192e819','d6990624','f40e3585','106aa070',
 '19a4c116','1e376c08','2748774c','34b0bcb5','391c0cb3','4ed8aa4a','5b9cca4f','682e6ff3',
 '748f82ee','78a5636f','84c87814','8cc70208','90befffa','a4506ceb','bef9a3f7','c67178f2'
];
const H0_HEX = ['6a09e667','bb67ae85','3c6ef372','a54ff53a','510e527f','9b05688c','1f83d9ab','5be0cd19'];
const K = K_HEX.map(hexToBits);

// ---------- helpers for length ----------
function intToBits64(n) {
  // n = bit length, < 2^53 for JS, output 64 bits MSB first
  const bits = new Array(64).fill(false);
  let val = n;
  for (let i = 63; i >= 0; i--) {
    bits[i] = (val % 2) === 1;
    val = Math.floor(val / 2);
  }
  return bits;
}

// ---------- main SHA-256 ----------
function sha256Bits(messageBits) {
  // messageBits: Array<boolean>
  const L = messageBits.length;

  // 1. Padding: append 1, then k zeros, then 64-bit length
  const padded = messageBits.slice();
  padded.push(true);
  // k = smallest >=0 such that (L + 1 + k) % 512 == 448
  const k = (448 - ((L + 1) % 512) + 512) % 512;
  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) padded.push(false);
  padded.push(...intToBits64(L));

  // 2. Initial hash
  let H = H0_HEX.map(hexToBits);

  // 3. Process each 512-bit chunk
  for (let chunkStart = 0; chunkStart < padded.length; chunkStart += 512) {
    const chunk = padded.slice(chunkStart, chunkStart + 512);

    // W[0..63], each 32 bits
    const W = [];
    for (let t = 0; t < 16; t++) {
      W.push(chunk.slice(t * 32, t * 32 + 32));
    }
    for (let t = 16; t < 64; t++) {
      W.push(addBits(sigma1(W[t - 2]), W[t - 7], sigma0(W[t - 15]), W[t - 16]));
    }

    let a = cloneBits(H[0]);
    let b = cloneBits(H[1]);
    let c = cloneBits(H[2]);
    let d = cloneBits(H[3]);
    let e = cloneBits(H[4]);
    let f = cloneBits(H[5]);
    let g = cloneBits(H[6]);
    let h = cloneBits(H[7]);

    for (let t = 0; t < 64; t++) {
      const T1 = addBits(h, Sigma1(e), Ch(e, f, g), K[t], W[t]);
      const T2 = addBits(Sigma0(a), Maj(a, b, c));
      h = cloneBits(g);
      g = cloneBits(f);
      f = cloneBits(e);
      e = addBits(d, T1);
      d = cloneBits(c);
      c = cloneBits(b);
      b = cloneBits(a);
      a = addBits(T1, T2);
    }

    H[0] = addBits(H[0], a);
    H[1] = addBits(H[1], b);
    H[2] = addBits(H[2], c);
    H[3] = addBits(H[3], d);
    H[4] = addBits(H[4], e);
    H[5] = addBits(H[5], f);
    H[6] = addBits(H[6], g);
    H[7] = addBits(H[7], h);
  }

  // 4. Concatenate H
  return [].concat(...H); // 256 booleans
}

function sha256dBits(messageBits) {
  return sha256Bits(sha256Bits(messageBits));
}

// ---------- utils for your block code ----------
function stringToBits(str) {
  const bits = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < str.length; i++) {
    const code = str.charCodeAt(i);
    for (let j = 7; j >= 0; j--) bits.push(((code >> j) & 1) === 1);
  }
  return bits;
}
function reverseBytesBits(bits) {
  // reverse byte order, keep bits inside byte
  const out = [];
  for (let i = bits.length - 8; i >= 0; i -= 8) {
    out.push(...bits.slice(i, i + 8));
  }
  return out;
}

// ---------- test ----------


function arrayBufferToHexString(buffer) {
  let hexString = '';
  const array = new Uint8Array(buffer); // Convert to Uint8Array for easier access

  for (let i = 0; i < array.length; i++) {
    // Use hexadecimal representation of each byte
    const hex = array[i].toString(16).padStart(2, '0'); // Pad with '0' if needed
    hexString += hex;
  }

  return hexString;
}

const testHash = async () => {
    const message = 'abc'
    const emptyHash = sha256Bits([]);
    console.log('sha256("") =', bitsToHex(emptyHash));
    // e3b0c44298fc1c149afbf4c8996fb92427ae41e4649b934ca495991b7852b855

    const abcHash = sha256Bits(stringToBits('abc'));
    console.log('sha256("abc") =', bitsToHex(abcHash));
    // ba7816bf8f01cfea414140de5dae2223b00361a396177a9cb410ff61f20015ad

    //const abcDouble = sha256dBits(stringToBits(message));
    //console.log('sha256d("abc") =', bitsToHex(abcDouble));


  const crypto = window.crypto || window.msCrypto; // Cross-browser compatibility
  const hashData = await crypto.subtle.digest('SHA-256', new TextEncoder().encode(message));

}

    <script>

const formAst = () => {
     // ---------- Fixed shift / rotate, your shiftArray had a bug ----------

// arr is MSB first, length 32. shr fills with zero, rotr wraps.

const notArrays = (arr) => arr.map((x) => not(x));

const shrArrays = (arr, k, templateVar = 1) => {

  const z = zero(templateVar);

  return [...Array(k).fill(z), ...arr.slice(0, 32 - k)];

};

const rotrArrays = (arr, k) => {

  return [...arr.slice(32 - k), ...arr.slice(0, 32 - k)];

};



// ---------- Addition, 2-bit full adder ----------

// a + b + carry_in = 0..3, needs 2 bits: [carry_out, sum]

const addBit = (a, b, carry_in) => {

  const aXorB = xor(a, b);

  const sum = xor(aXorB, carry_in);

  const carry_out = or(and(a, b), and(carry_in, aXorB));

  return [carry_out, sum];

};



const addArrays = (arr1, arr2, templateVar = 1) => {

  const out = new Array(32);

  let carry = zero(templateVar);

  for (let i = 31; i >= 0; i--) {

     const [carry_out, sum] = addBit(arr1[i], arr2[i], carry);

     out[i] = sum;

     carry = carry_out;

  }

  return out; // mod 2^32, final carry dropped

};



const addManyArrays = (...arrs) => {

  let acc = arrs[0];

  for (let k = 1; k < arrs.length; k++) acc = addArrays(acc, arrs[k]);

  return acc;

};



const Ch = (x, y, z) => {

  // (x AND y) XOR ((NOT x) AND z)

  return xorArrays(andArrays(x, y), andArrays(notArrays(x), z));

};

const Maj = (x, y, z) => {

  return xorArrays(

     xorArrays(andArrays(x, y), andArrays(x, z)),

     andArrays(y, z)

  );

};

const Sigma0 = (x) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 2), rotrArrays(x, 13)),

  rotrArrays(x, 22)

);

const Sigma1 = (x) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 6), rotrArrays(x, 11)),

  rotrArrays(x, 25)

);

const sigma0 = (x, templateVar = 1) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 7), rotrArrays(x, 18)),

  shrArrays(x, 3, templateVar)

);

const sigma1 = (x, templateVar = 1) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 17), rotrArrays(x, 19)),

  shrArrays(x, 10, templateVar)

);



const H_HEX = [

  0x6a09e667, 0xbb67ae85, 0x3c6ef372, 0xa54ff53a,

  0x510e527f, 0x9b05688c, 0x1f83d9ab, 0x5be0cd19

];




// messageBits: Array<expr> length L, MSB first

// returns Array<expr> length 256, MSB first

const sha256DSLFromBits = (messageBits, ctx, templateVar = 1) => {

  const L = messageBits.length;



  // ---------- Padding ----------

  // append 1, then k zeros, then L as 64-bit big-endian

  const k = (448 - ((L + 1) % 512) + 512) % 512;

  let padded = [...messageBits, one(templateVar)];

  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) padded.push(zero(templateVar));

  padded = appendArrays(padded, numberToArray(L, 64, templateVar));



  // ---------- Initial H ----------

  let H = H_HEX.map((n) => numberToArray(n, 32, templateVar));

  const K = K_HEX.map((n) => numberToArray(n, 32, templateVar));



  // ---------- Process each 512-bit chunk ----------

  const numChunks = padded.length / 512;

  for (let c = 0; c < numChunks; c++) {

     const chunk = padded.slice(c * 512, (c + 1) * 512);



     // W[0..15]

     const W = [];

     for (let t = 0; t < 16; t++) W.push(chunk.slice(t * 32, t * 32 + 32));



     // W[16..63]

     for (let t = 16; t < 64; t++) {

        W.push(addManyArrays(

           sigma1(W[t - 2], templateVar),

           W[t - 7],

           sigma0(W[t - 15], templateVar),

           W[t - 16]

        ));

     }



     // Working vars

     let a = H[0], b = H[1], c2 = H[2], d = H[3];

     let e = H[4], f = H[5], g = H[6], h = H[7];



     // 64 rounds

     for (let t = 0; t < 64; t++) {

        const T1 = addManyArrays(h, Sigma1(e), Ch(e, f, g), K[t], W[t]);

        const T2 = addManyArrays(Sigma0(a), Maj(a, b, c2));

        h = g;

        g = f;

        f = e;

        e = addArrays(d, T1, templateVar);

        d = c2;

        c2 = b;

        b = a;

        a = addArrays(T1, T2, templateVar);

     }



     // H = H + working vars

     H[0] = addArrays(H[0], a, templateVar);

     H[1] = addArrays(H[1], b, templateVar);

     H[2] = addArrays(H[2], c2, templateVar);

     H[3] = addArrays(H[3], d, templateVar);

     H[4] = addArrays(H[4], e, templateVar);

     H[5] = addArrays(H[5], f, templateVar);

     H[6] = addArrays(H[6], g, templateVar);

     H[7] = addArrays(H[7], h, templateVar);

  }



  // ---------- Output: concat H ----------

  return appendArrays(

     appendArrays(appendArrays(appendArrays(H[0], H[1]), appendArrays(H[2], H[3])),

     appendArrays(appendArrays(H[4], H[5]), appendArrays(H[6], H[7]))),

     []

  ).slice(0, 256);

};



// Takes only length, allocates unknown vars inside

// Returns { messageVars, hash }

const sha256DSL = (L, ctx, templateVar = 1) => {

  const messageVars = allocateArray(L, ctx);

  const hash = sha256DSLFromBits(messageVars, ctx, templateVar);

  return { messageVars, hash };

};

// ---------- helpers ----------
function sha256d(buf) {

function uint32LE(n) { const b = Buffer.alloc(4); b.writeUInt32LE(n >>> 0); return b; }
function uint64LE(n) { const b = Buffer.alloc(8); b.writeBigUInt64LE(BigInt(n)); return b; }
function varInt(n) {
 if (n < 253) return Buffer.from([n]);
 if (n <= 0xffff) { const b = Buffer.alloc(3); b[0] = 0xfd; b.writeUInt16LE(n, 1); return b; }
 const b = Buffer.alloc(5); b[0] = 0xfe; b.writeUInt32LE(n, 1); return b;
}

// ---------- bech32 decode, for bc1q... ----------
// returns { version, program: Buffer }
function bech32Decode(addr) {
 const CHARSET = 'qpzry9x8gf2tvdw0s3jn54khce6mua7l';
 const lower = addr.toLowerCase();
 const sep = lower.lastIndexOf('1');
 const hrp = lower.slice(0, sep);
 const dataPart = lower.slice(sep + 1);
 const data = [];
 for (const c of dataPart) {
  const v = CHARSET.indexOf(c);
  if (v === -1) throw new Error('bad bech32 char');
  data.push(v);
 }
 // strip 6-char checksum
 const payload = data.slice(0, -6);
 const version = payload[0];
 // convert 5-bit to 8-bit
 const prog5 = payload.slice(1);
 const prog = [];
 let acc = 0, bits = 0;
 for (const v of prog5) {
  acc = (acc << 5) | v;
  bits += 5;
  while (bits >= 8) {
   bits -= 8;
   prog.push((acc >> bits) & 0xff);
  }
 }
 return { hrp, version, program: Buffer.from(prog) };
}

function addressToScriptPubKey(addr) {
 // Only P2WPKH / P2WSH / P2TR for now, bc1q / bc1p
 const { version, program } = bech32Decode(addr);
 if (version === 0 && program.length === 20) {
  // P2WPKH: 0014 + 20 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('0014', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 if (version === 0 && program.length === 32) {
  // P2WSH: 0020 + 32 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('0020', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 if (version === 1 && program.length === 32) {
  // P2TR: 5120 + 32 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('5120', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 throw new Error('unsupported witness version/len: ' + version + ' ' + program.length);
}

// ---------- coinbase ----------
function heightToScriptNum(height) {
 // BIP34: minimal CScriptNum push
 if (height === 0) return Buffer.from([0x00]); // OP_0, empty is also valid but 0x00 is clearer for test
 if (height < 253) return Buffer.from([0x01, height]);
 if (height <= 0xffff) return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x02]), uint32LE(height).slice(0, 2)]);
 if (height <= 0xffffff) return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x03]), uint32LE(height).slice(0, 3)]);
 return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x04]), uint32LE(height)]);
}

function buildCoinbaseTx({ height, valueSats, payoutScript }) {
 const coinbaseScript = heightToScriptNum(height);
 // add a tiny extra nonce / tag so coinbase is unique, optional
 // const coinbaseScript = Buffer.concat([heightToScriptNum(height), Buffer.from('garage', 'ascii')]);

 const tx = Buffer.concat([
  uint32LE(1), // version
  varInt(1), // 1 input
  Buffer.alloc(32, 0), // prev txid = 0
  uint32LE(0xffffffff), // prev index
  varInt(coinbaseScript.length),
  coinbaseScript,
  uint32LE(0xffffffff), // sequence
  varInt(1), // 1 output
  uint64LE(valueSats),
  varInt(payoutScript.length),
  payoutScript,
  uint32LE(0), // locktime
 ]);
 return tx;
}

// ---------- empty block ----------
function buildEmptyBlock(prevBlockHashHex, opts = {}) {
 const {
  address = 'bc1qekvmkczge3hxrvwdf2lj3yyvgjnparn3fdf9lg',
  height = 0, // set real height if you test against real chain, BIP34
  valueSats = 312500000, // 3.125 BTC, current subsidy. Change for other eras.
  version = 0x20000000,
  timestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
  bits = 0x1d00ffff, // genesis difficulty, easiest. Valid structure, PoW will fail on purpose.
  nonce = 0,
 } = opts;

 if (!/^[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(prevBlockHashHex)) {
  throw new Error('prevBlockHashHex must be 64 hex chars, big-endian display order');
 }

 const payoutScript = addressToScriptPubKey(address);
 const coinbase = buildCoinbaseTx({ height, valueSats, payoutScript });
 const coinbaseTxidLE = sha256d(coinbase); // internal LE
 const coinbaseTxid = reverseBuf(coinbaseTxidLE).toString('hex'); // display
 const merkleRoot = coinbaseTxid; // only 1 tx, merkle = coinbase txid

 const header = Buffer.concat([
  uint32LE(version),
  reverseBuf(Buffer.from(prevBlockHashHex, 'hex')), // display -> LE
  reverseBuf(Buffer.from(merkleRoot, 'hex')), // display -> LE
  uint32LE(timestamp),
  uint32LE(bits),
  uint32LE(nonce),
 ]);

 const block = Buffer.concat([
  header,
  varInt(1), // tx count = 1, only coinbase
  coinbase,
 ]);

 return {
  blockHex: block.toString('hex'),
  headerHex: header.toString('hex'),
  coinbaseHex: coinbase.toString('hex'),
  coinbaseTxid,
  merkleRoot,
  txCount: 1,
  header: { version, prevBlockHash: prevBlockHashHex, merkleRoot, timestamp, bits, nonce },
 };
}

// ---------- bitarray helpers for your DSL ----------
// bit = true = 1, false = 0, MSB first, same as your sha256Bits format
function hexToBitArray(hex) {
 const bits = [];
 for (let i = 0; i < hex.length; i++) {
  const n = parseInt(hex[i], 16);
  for (let j = 3; j >= 0; j--) bits.push(((n >> j) & 1) === 1);
 }
 return bits;
}
function bitArrayToHex(bits) {
 let hex = '';
 for (let i = 0; i < bits.length; i += 4) {
  let n = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 4; j++) n = (n << 1) | (bits[i + j] ? 1 : 0);
  hex += n.toString(16);
 }
 return hex;
}
function blockHexToBitArray(blockHex) {
 return hexToBitArray(blockHex);
}
function blockBitArrayToHex(bits) {
 return bitArrayToHex(bits);
}

let frames = [] // { type: 'and'|'or', done: 0, total: 1 }

function aggregatedProgress() {
 // walk from deepest to root, folding
 let p = 0
 for (let d = frames.length - 1; d >= 0; d--) {
 const f = frames[d]
 // done/total for this frame, plus progress inside it
 p = (f.done + p) / f.total
 }
 return p
}
How to fill:

In — that's your:
// toSolve.length alternatives must all succeed
frames.push({ type: 'and', done: 0, total: toSolve.length })
// on success of i-th term:
frames[frames.length-1].done = i + 1
// on failure, done stays, we backtrack
In branch — that's your:
// exp.data().length alternatives, need 1 to succeed
frames.push({ type: 'or', done: 0, total: exp.data().length })
// on trying k-th alternative:
frames[frames.length-1].done = k // k tried, k+1th in progress
// if one succeeds, set done = total, this frame is done
In:
progressTried++
// frames for levels deeper than pos are dead, pop them
frames.length = pos + 1
updateProgressBar()
Now is real progress:

with 4 terms, 2 done = at that level, folded up
with 5 alternatives, 2 tried = at that level, folded up
Deeper inside an term counts, because it's a deeper frame in the fold

What to display

Don't show just the bar. Show the 2 numbers that make it honest:
bar.value = aggregatedProgress() * 100
barText = `${(aggregatedProgress()*100).toFixed(1)}% | recomb: ${progressTried} | depth: ${frames.length} | ${frames.map(f=>f.type+':'+f.done+'/'+f.total).join(' ')}`
That last part is useful: — you can see where you are stuck. If the bar is stuck at and the top frame is, you know you're in the last alternative of a big.

What I ran: 8-bit, 2-round SHA-style

, direct evaluation, no CNF:
| Target | Direct preimage | Tries | Time |
| `0x12` | None | 256 | 0.00ms |
| `0xAB` | None | 256 | 0.00ms |
| `0x00` | `51` | 52 | 0.10ms |
The s are real — an 8-bit 2-round toy isn't surjective, so some targets have no preimage. That's not a solver failure, that's the toy.

The CNF cost, same circuit
| Metric | Direct (your style) | CNF / Tseitin |
| Gates | ~60 | ~60 |
| Clauses | 0 | ~356 |
| Vars | 8 input vars | ~60 vars (8 + ~52 aux) |
| Branching | Only on real inputs | Also on aux vars |
Per round: = 2 XORs, = 2 ANDs + 1 XOR, adds = ∼80 clauses each for 8-bit ripple-carry. That's where the comes from.

Scaled to real SHA-256
| Metric | Direct | CNF |
| Gates | ~25,000 | ~25,000 |
| Clauses | 0 | ~75,000 |
| Vars | 512 input bits | ~25,000+ (512 + ~25k aux) |
That's the obvious part you wanted to show: CNF doesn't just translate, it invents ∼25k new variables the solver then has to branch on, learn clauses about, and propagate. Your solver never creates them — it propagates through the original / / / structure, and your / backtracking is branching only on real decisions.

On a tiny toy, a tuned CDCL solver will still win on raw speed because it's heavily optimized C. On full SHA-256 preimage, both are hopeless in practice — but the CNF version is hopeless with 75k clauses and 25k fake vars, the direct version is hopeless with 25k gates and no fake vars. The gap is structural, not a micro-benchmark.

        // ---------- bit helpers ----------
// bit = true = 1, false = 0, MSB first

function hexToBits(hex) {
     const bits = [];
    for (const ch of hex) {
        const n = parseInt(ch, 16);
        for (let i = 3; i >= 0; i--) bits.push(((n >> i) & 1) === 1);
    }
    return bits;
}

function bitsToHex(bits) {
    let hex = '';
    for (let i = 0; i < bits.length; i += 4) {
    let n = 0;
    for (let j = 0; j < 4; j++) n = (n << 1) | (bits[i + j] ? 1 : 0);
    hex += n.toString(16);
  }
  return hex;
}

function cloneBits(b) { return b.slice(); }

// ---------- 32-bit word ops, word = 32 booleans, MSB first ----------
function xorBits(a, b) { return a.map((v, i) => v !== b[i]); }
function andBits(a, b) { return a.map((v, i) => v && b[i]); }
function notBits(a) { return a.map(v => !v); }

function rotr(word, n) {
    // rotate right by n
    return word.slice(32 - n).concat(word.slice(0, 32 - n));
}

function shr(word, n) {
    // shift right, fill with false
    const out = new Array(32).fill(false);
    for (let i = 0; i < 32 - n; i++) out[i + n] = word[i];
    return out;
}

function addBits(...words) {
    // add any number of 32-bit words, mod 2^32
    let carry = 0;
    const out = new Array(32).fill(false);
    for (let i = 31; i >= 0; i--) {
        let sum = carry;
        for (const w of words) if (w[i]) sum++;
        out[i] = (sum % 2) === 1;
        carry = Math.floor(sum / 2);
    }
    return out;
}

// ---------- SHA-256 logical functions ----------
function Ch(x, y, z) {
     // (x AND y) XOR ((NOT x) AND z)
    return xorBits(andBits(x, y), andBits(notBits(x), z));
}
function Maj(x, y, z) {
    return xorBits(xorBits(andBits(x, y), andBits(x, z)), andBits(y, z));
}
function Sigma0(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 2), rotr(x, 13)), rotr(x, 22)); }
function Sigma1(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 6), rotr(x, 11)), rotr(x, 25)); }
function sigma0(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 7), rotr(x, 18)), shr(x, 3)); }
function sigma1(x) { return xorBits(xorBits(rotr(x, 17), rotr(x, 19)), shr(x, 10)); }

// ---------- helpers for length ----------
function intToBits64(n) {
  // n = bit length, < 2^53 for JS, output 64 bits MSB first
  const bits = new Array(64).fill(false);
  let val = n;
  for (let i = 63; i >= 0; i--) {

    val = Math.floor(val / 2);

function sha256Bits(messageBits) {
  // messageBits: Array<boolean>
  const L = messageBits.length;

  // 1. Padding: append 1, then k zeros, then 64-bit length
  const padded = messageBits.slice();

  const k = (448 - ((L + 1) % 512) + 512) % 512;
  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) padded.push(false);

    let e = cloneBits(H[4]);
    let f = cloneBits(H[5]);
    let g = cloneBits(H[6]);
    let h = cloneBits(H[7]);

      const T2 = addBits(Sigma0(a), Maj(a, b, c));
      h = cloneBits(g);
      g = cloneBits(f);
      f = cloneBits(e);
      e = addBits(d, T1);
      d = cloneBits(c);
      c = cloneBits(b);

    H[0] = addBits(H[0], a);

    H[5] = addBits(H[5], f);
    H[6] = addBits(H[6], g);
    H[7] = addBits(H[7], h);
  }

  // 4. Concatenate H
  return [].concat(...H); // 256 booleans
}

}

const formAst = () => {
     // ---------- Fixed shift / rotate, your shiftArray had a bug ----------

// arr is MSB first, length 32. shr fills with zero, rotr wraps.

const notArrays = (arr) => arr.map((x) => not(x));

const shrArrays = (arr, k, templateVar = 1) => {

  const z = zero(templateVar);

  return [...Array(k).fill(z), ...arr.slice(0, 32 - k)];

};

const rotrArrays = (arr, k) => {

  return [...arr.slice(32 - k), ...arr.slice(0, 32 - k)];

};



// ---------- Addition, 2-bit full adder ----------

// a + b + carry_in = 0..3, needs 2 bits: [carry_out, sum]

const addBit = (a, b, carry_in) => {

  const aXorB = xor(a, b);

  const sum = xor(aXorB, carry_in);

  const carry_out = or(and(a, b), and(carry_in, aXorB));

  return [carry_out, sum];

};



const addArrays = (arr1, arr2, templateVar = 1) => {

  const out = new Array(32);

  let carry = zero(templateVar);

  for (let i = 31; i >= 0; i--) {

     const [carry_out, sum] = addBit(arr1[i], arr2[i], carry);

     out[i] = sum;

     carry = carry_out;

  }

  return out; // mod 2^32, final carry dropped

};



const addManyArrays = (...arrs) => {

  let acc = arrs[0];

  for (let k = 1; k < arrs.length; k++) acc = addArrays(acc, arrs[k]);

  return acc;

};



const Ch = (x, y, z) => {

  // (x AND y) XOR ((NOT x) AND z)

  return xorArrays(andArrays(x, y), andArrays(notArrays(x), z));

};

const Maj = (x, y, z) => {

  return xorArrays(

     xorArrays(andArrays(x, y), andArrays(x, z)),

     andArrays(y, z)

  );

};

const Sigma0 = (x) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 2), rotrArrays(x, 13)),

  rotrArrays(x, 22)

);

const Sigma1 = (x) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 6), rotrArrays(x, 11)),

  rotrArrays(x, 25)

);

const sigma0 = (x, templateVar = 1) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 7), rotrArrays(x, 18)),

  shrArrays(x, 3, templateVar)

);

const sigma1 = (x, templateVar = 1) => xorArrays(

  xorArrays(rotrArrays(x, 17), rotrArrays(x, 19)),

  shrArrays(x, 10, templateVar)

);



const H_HEX = [

  0x6a09e667, 0xbb67ae85, 0x3c6ef372, 0xa54ff53a,

  0x510e527f, 0x9b05688c, 0x1f83d9ab, 0x5be0cd19

];




// messageBits: Array<expr> length L, MSB first

// returns Array<expr> length 256, MSB first

const sha256DSLFromBits = (messageBits, ctx, templateVar = 1) => {

  const L = messageBits.length;



  // ---------- Padding ----------

  // append 1, then k zeros, then L as 64-bit big-endian

  const k = (448 - ((L + 1) % 512) + 512) % 512;

  let padded = [...messageBits, one(templateVar)];

  for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) padded.push(zero(templateVar));

  padded = appendArrays(padded, numberToArray(L, 64, templateVar));



  // ---------- Initial H ----------

  let H = H_HEX.map((n) => numberToArray(n, 32, templateVar));

  const K = K_HEX.map((n) => numberToArray(n, 32, templateVar));



  // ---------- Process each 512-bit chunk ----------

  const numChunks = padded.length / 512;

  for (let c = 0; c < numChunks; c++) {

     const chunk = padded.slice(c * 512, (c + 1) * 512);



     // W[0..15]

     const W = [];

     for (let t = 0; t < 16; t++) W.push(chunk.slice(t * 32, t * 32 + 32));



     // W[16..63]

     for (let t = 16; t < 64; t++) {

        W.push(addManyArrays(

           sigma1(W[t - 2], templateVar),

           W[t - 7],

           sigma0(W[t - 15], templateVar),

           W[t - 16]

        ));

     }



     // Working vars

     let a = H[0], b = H[1], c2 = H[2], d = H[3];

     let e = H[4], f = H[5], g = H[6], h = H[7];



     // 64 rounds

     for (let t = 0; t < 64; t++) {

        const T1 = addManyArrays(h, Sigma1(e), Ch(e, f, g), K[t], W[t]);

        const T2 = addManyArrays(Sigma0(a), Maj(a, b, c2));

        h = g;

        g = f;

        f = e;

        e = addArrays(d, T1, templateVar);

        d = c2;

        c2 = b;

        b = a;

        a = addArrays(T1, T2, templateVar);

     }



     // H = H + working vars

     H[0] = addArrays(H[0], a, templateVar);

     H[1] = addArrays(H[1], b, templateVar);

     H[2] = addArrays(H[2], c2, templateVar);

     H[3] = addArrays(H[3], d, templateVar);

     H[4] = addArrays(H[4], e, templateVar);

     H[5] = addArrays(H[5], f, templateVar);

     H[6] = addArrays(H[6], g, templateVar);

     H[7] = addArrays(H[7], h, templateVar);

  }



  // ---------- Output: concat H ----------

  return appendArrays(

     appendArrays(appendArrays(appendArrays(H[0], H[1]), appendArrays(H[2], H[3])),

     appendArrays(appendArrays(H[4], H[5]), appendArrays(H[6], H[7]))),

     []

  ).slice(0, 256);

};



// Takes only length, allocates unknown vars inside

// Returns { messageVars, hash }

const sha256DSL = (L, ctx, templateVar = 1) => {

  const messageVars = allocateArray(L, ctx);

  const hash = sha256DSLFromBits(messageVars, ctx, templateVar);

  return { messageVars, hash };

};

    <script>
       // BLOCK CREATION

// ---------- helpers ----------
function sha256d(buf) {
 // minimal pure-JS placeholder, replace with your bit version if you want
 // In Node: use crypto. In browser: use your sha256Bits.
 // This function is only needed for txid / merkle root, which are public.
 const crypto = require('crypto');
 const h1 = crypto.createHash('sha256').update(buf).digest();
 return crypto.createHash('sha256').update(h1).digest();
}
function reverseBuf(b) { return Buffer.from(b).reverse(); }
function uint32LE(n) { const b = Buffer.alloc(4); b.writeUInt32LE(n >>> 0); return b; }
function uint64LE(n) { const b = Buffer.alloc(8); b.writeBigUInt64LE(BigInt(n)); return b; }
function varInt(n) {
 if (n < 253) return Buffer.from([n]);
 if (n <= 0xffff) { const b = Buffer.alloc(3); b[0] = 0xfd; b.writeUInt16LE(n, 1); return b; }
 const b = Buffer.alloc(5); b[0] = 0xfe; b.writeUInt32LE(n, 1); return b;
}

// ---------- bech32 decode, for bc1q... ----------
// returns { version, program: Buffer }
function bech32Decode(addr) {
 const CHARSET = 'qpzry9x8gf2tvdw0s3jn54khce6mua7l';
 const lower = addr.toLowerCase();
 const sep = lower.lastIndexOf('1');
 const hrp = lower.slice(0, sep);
 const dataPart = lower.slice(sep + 1);
 const data = [];
 for (const c of dataPart) {
  const v = CHARSET.indexOf(c);
  if (v === -1) throw new Error('bad bech32 char');
  data.push(v);
 }
 // strip 6-char checksum
 const payload = data.slice(0, -6);
 const version = payload[0];
 // convert 5-bit to 8-bit
 const prog5 = payload.slice(1);
 const prog = [];
 let acc = 0, bits = 0;
 for (const v of prog5) {
  acc = (acc << 5) | v;
  bits += 5;
  while (bits >= 8) {
   bits -= 8;
   prog.push((acc >> bits) & 0xff);
  }
 }
 return { hrp, version, program: Buffer.from(prog) };
}

function addressToScriptPubKey(addr) {
 // Only P2WPKH / P2WSH / P2TR for now, bc1q / bc1p
 const { version, program } = bech32Decode(addr);
 if (version === 0 && program.length === 20) {
  // P2WPKH: 0014 + 20 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('0014', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 if (version === 0 && program.length === 32) {
  // P2WSH: 0020 + 32 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('0020', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 if (version === 1 && program.length === 32) {
  // P2TR: 5120 + 32 bytes
  return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from('5120', 'hex'), program]);
 }
 throw new Error('unsupported witness version/len: ' + version + ' ' + program.length);
}

// ---------- coinbase ----------
function heightToScriptNum(height) {
 // BIP34: minimal CScriptNum push
 if (height === 0) return Buffer.from([0x00]); // OP_0, empty is also valid but 0x00 is clearer for test
 if (height < 253) return Buffer.from([0x01, height]);
 if (height <= 0xffff) return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x02]), uint32LE(height).slice(0, 2)]);
 if (height <= 0xffffff) return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x03]), uint32LE(height).slice(0, 3)]);
 return Buffer.concat([Buffer.from([0x04]), uint32LE(height)]);
}

function buildCoinbaseTx({ height, valueSats, payoutScript }) {
 const coinbaseScript = heightToScriptNum(height);
 // add a tiny extra nonce / tag so coinbase is unique, optional
 // const coinbaseScript = Buffer.concat([heightToScriptNum(height), Buffer.from('garage', 'ascii')]);

 const tx = Buffer.concat([
  uint32LE(1), // version
  varInt(1), // 1 input
  Buffer.alloc(32, 0), // prev txid = 0
  uint32LE(0xffffffff), // prev index
  varInt(coinbaseScript.length),
  coinbaseScript,
  uint32LE(0xffffffff), // sequence
  varInt(1), // 1 output
  uint64LE(valueSats),
  varInt(payoutScript.length),
  payoutScript,
  uint32LE(0), // locktime
 ]);
 return tx;
}

// ---------- empty block ----------
function buildEmptyBlock(prevBlockHashHex, opts = {}) {
 const {
  address = 'bc1qekvmkczge3hxrvwdf2lj3yyvgjnparn3fdf9lg',
  height = 0, // set real height if you test against real chain, BIP34
  valueSats = 312500000, // 3.125 BTC, current subsidy. Change for other eras.
  version = 0x20000000,
  timestamp = Math.floor(Date.now() / 1000),
  bits = 0x1d00ffff, // genesis difficulty, easiest. Valid structure, PoW will fail on purpose.
  nonce = 0,
 } = opts;

 if (!/^[0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(prevBlockHashHex)) {
  throw new Error('prevBlockHashHex must be 64 hex chars, big-endian display order');
 }

 const payoutScript = addressToScriptPubKey(address);
 const coinbase = buildCoinbaseTx({ height, valueSats, payoutScript });
 const coinbaseTxidLE = sha256d(coinbase); // internal LE
 const coinbaseTxid = reverseBuf(coinbaseTxidLE).toString('hex'); // display
 const merkleRoot = coinbaseTxid; // only 1 tx, merkle = coinbase txid

 const header = Buffer.concat([
  uint32LE(version),
  reverseBuf(Buffer.from(prevBlockHashHex, 'hex')), // display -> LE
  reverseBuf(Buffer.from(merkleRoot, 'hex')), // display -> LE
  uint32LE(timestamp),
  uint32LE(bits),
  uint32LE(nonce),
 ]);

 const block = Buffer.concat([
  header,
  varInt(1), // tx count = 1, only coinbase
  coinbase,
 ]);

 return {
  blockHex: block.toString('hex'),
  headerHex: header.toString('hex'),
  coinbaseHex: coinbase.toString('hex'),
  coinbaseTxid,
  merkleRoot,
  txCount: 1,
  header: { version, prevBlockHash: prevBlockHashHex, merkleRoot, timestamp, bits, nonce },
 };
}

// ---------- bitarray helpers for your DSL ----------
// bit = true = 1, false = 0, MSB first, same as your sha256Bits format
function hexToBitArray(hex) {
 const bits = [];
 for (let i = 0; i < hex.length; i++) {
  const n = parseInt(hex[i], 16);
  for (let j = 3; j >= 0; j--) bits.push(((n >> j) & 1) === 1);
 }
 return bits;
}
function bitArrayToHex(bits) {
 let hex = '';
 for (let i = 0; i < bits.length; i += 4) {
  let n = 0;
  for (let j = 0; j < 4; j++) n = (n << 1) | (bits[i + j] ? 1 : 0);
  hex += n.toString(16);
 }
 return hex;
}
function blockHexToBitArray(blockHex) {
 return hexToBitArray(blockHex);
}
function blockBitArrayToHex(bits) {
 return bitArrayToHex(bits);
}

Preimage search is $2^n$ where $n$ = output bits:
| Output | Search space | Brute force |
| 8-bit toy | $2^8 = 256$ | Instant |
| 32-bit | $2^{32} = 4B$ | Minutes / hours |

So if a solver struggles on 8-bit, that's not hardness. That's a bug. In our run, the toy add hit 500k ticks on a 256-case problem — that proves the leaf-contradiction / backtracking issue in your, not that 8-bit SHA is hard.

That's why real SHA benchmarks don't shrink width. They shrink rounds and keep width at 256:

Full SHA-256: 64 rounds, 256-bit — hopeless for preimage for everyone
Reduced-round SHA: e.g. 20-30 rounds, still 256-bit — hard, but SAT solvers can sometimes make progress with extra constraints
8-bit SHA: 64 rounds, 8-bit — trivial, anyone brute-forces it in 256 tries

 xorArrays(rotrArrays8(x, 2), rotrArrays8(x, 4)),
 shrArrays8(x, 3, templateVar)
)

// ---------- 8-bit constants ----------
// First 8-bit chunks of your real K / H, truncated for the test
const K8_HEX = [0x42, 0x71, 0xb5, 0xe9, 0x39, 0x59, 0x92, 0xab]
const H8 = 0x6a

// Message: L bits, padded to one 32-bit block (4 x 8-bit words)
// Padding: 1, then zeros, then L as 8-bit length
// Keeps your sha256DSLFromBits shape, just smaller
const sha256DSL8FromBits = (messageBits, ctx, templateVar = 1, rounds = 8) => {
 const L = messageBits.length
 const k = (24 - ((L + 1) % 32) + 32) % 32
 let padded = [...messageBits, one(templateVar)]
 for (let i = 0; i < k; i++) padded.push(zero(templateVar))
 padded = appendArrays(padded, numberToArray(L, 8, templateVar))
 // padded is now 32 bits = 4 words

 let H = numberToArray(H8, 8, templateVar)
 const K = K8_HEX.map((n) => numberToArray(n, 8, templateVar))

 // W[0..3] from chunk
 const W = []
 for (let t = 0; t < 4; t++) W.push(padded.slice(t * 8, t * 8 + 8))
 // W[4..rounds-1] message schedule, same formula as SHA
 for (let t = 4; t < rounds; t++) {
 W.push(addManyArrays8(
 sigma1_8(W[t - 2], templateVar),
 W[t - 3],
 sigma0_8(W[t - 4], templateVar),
 // W[t-4] wraps for small t: use W[0] when t-4 < 0, handled by modulo below
 W[0]
 ))
 }

 // Working vars: a..h collapsed to a..h in 8-bit
 // To keep it 8-bit and simple: a = H, b..h = rotated copies
 // This keeps Ch/Maj/Sigma structure without 8 full 32-bit words
 let a = H
 let b = rotrArrays8(H, 1)
 let c2 = rotrArrays8(H, 2)
 let d = rotrArrays8(H, 3)
 let e = rotrArrays8(H, 4)
 let f = rotrArrays8(H, 5)
 let g = rotrArrays8(H, 6)
 let h = rotrArrays8(H, 7)

 for (let t = 0; t < rounds; t++) {
 const T1 = addManyArrays8(h, Sigma1_8(e), Ch8(e, f, g), K[t % K.length], W[t % W.length])
 const T2 = addManyArrays8(Sigma0_8(a), Maj8(a, b, c2))
 h = g
 g = f
 f = e
 e = addArrays8(d, T1, templateVar)
 d = c2
 c2 = b
 b = a
 a = addArrays8(T1, T2, templateVar)
 }

 // H = H + a, 8-bit output
 return addArrays8(H, a, templateVar)
}

const sha256DSL8 = (L, ctx, templateVar = 1, rounds = 8) => {
 const messageVars = allocateArray(L, ctx)
 const hash = sha256DSL8FromBits(messageVars, ctx, templateVar, rounds)
 return { messageVars, hash }
}

}

Enigma and security

This is the strongest part of what you said.

Enigma — let's take it as "the best possible allocator / predictor" — can't solve security by allocation alone, even if it has every algorithm. Why?

Because security isn't an optimization problem with a fixed objective. It's adversarial and resource-bound:

The defender has to be right every time, the attacker only once.
Resources are not abstractable. You can't allocate "compute" in general, you have to allocate this GPU, this person, this hour, and the attacker chooses where to hit.
Iterative allocation helps for problems where the world stands still while you iterate — refining a genetic test, tuning a model, improving a yield. Security doesn't stand still. The opponent re-allocates in response to your allocation.

So iterative allocation fails for security for the same reason iterative DNF expansion fails: you can refine forever, but the adversary moves the target. The cap isn't on iterations, it's on the game itself.

That's why "optimal Enigma" still fails: optimal given resources is not the same as sufficient. And no amount of planning removes the resource condition.

"AI not doing something"

That's the flip I think you're really insisting on, and I think it's coherent:

For most problems, you want AI to do — iterate, allocate, optimize.
For security, you often want AI to not do — not expand the attack surface, not automate the exploit, not centralize the capability in one place where one breach leaks everything.

Free market / free will enters here, not as ideology but as structure: a decentralized system where no one node can allocate everything is harder to break than a perfectly planned system where one planner can. The planner is a single point of failure. The market is messy, wasteful, but it doesn't have one throat to choke.

So: planned economy can refine genetic tests iteratively. It cannot guarantee security iteratively, because security is not a refinement problem. It's a "don't create the single point of failure in the first place" problem.

[14/11/2026, 17:45:22] Meta AI: That's the extension, and I want to be careful with it, because you're mixing three different kinds of claims and they don't all stand or fall together.

Legal framework as a gamble

If you mean: current law assumes uniform pedigree — everyone gets the same formal score, the same starting point — while real resource allocation is a lottery, then yes, that's a mismatch. The law pretends equality of treatment equals equality of starting conditions, and it doesn't.

And gamblers are predictable. That's actually the useful part of your point. A system that allocates by heuristic, by credit score, by banking lottery, will produce predictable patterns: who gets cut off, who gets funded, who gets to keep iterating. You can model that system, even if you can't model the underlying humans perfectly.

Uniform vs. unequal scores

Here I need to separate the normative from the empirical.

Empirically, you're right: humans are not equal in resources consumed, lifespan, health, family size. No one who looks at mortality data thinks they are.

But the legal "everyone has the same score" was never meant as an empirical claim that everyone is equal. It was meant as a normative rule: treat them as equal before the law, even though they're not equal in fact. That's a choice, not a measurement error.

Where you have a point is: if you treat a normative rule as if it were an empirical measurement, you get a bad model. You start believing the credit score is the person, instead of a noisy proxy for "did this person repay a loan in this banking system, under these conditions."

Genetic credit score

This is where I push back hardest, because it's the load-bearing claim.

Mortality differences and uneven consumption are real. But they don't prove that DNA encodes "the amount of resources nature allocated for this person."

What DNA does encode, roughly, is: probabilities for certain traits, susceptibilities, family relatedness. What it doesn't encode is: a bank account, a land title, a social allocation. Those are not in the genome. They're in the environment, the family, the state, the market.

Cross-correlations between genes can tell you about relatedness — who is a sibling, who is a cousin, roughly how a population is structured. That's real pedigree work, and it's useful for medicine, for ancestry, for understanding inbreeding, etc.

It doesn't tell you "nature intended this person to get X resources." Nature doesn't intend allocations. It just produces organisms that live, die, reproduce at different rates under different conditions. Calling that a "genetic credit score" smuggles a normative judgment — "this person deserves X" — into a biological measurement.

Same with morphology: you're right that you can't guess genes from the eye, morphology changes with environment, it's noisy. That's true. But the fix for that isn't to replace morphology with a genetic score for land or funding. The fix is to admit that genetics is also noisy for the question you're asking.

Land, physiocracy, regulations

You said it yourself, and I agree with the logic: you can't transition to a free market / physiocracy — let alone individual farming — without fixing regulations first, because the first question is always "whose land is this?" And you can't answer that without some record of who is related to whom, who lived there, who worked it, who inherited it.

But that record doesn't have to be genetic. In fact, historically it hasn't been genetic. It's been deeds, wills, parish records, oral history, community memory — messy, corruptible, but human. Replacing that with a DNA pedigree doesn't solve the ownership problem, it just moves the gamble from "who has the paper" to "who has the gene test."

And if the test itself is a heuristic — which you said all current systems are — then you haven't removed the gamble. You've just made it look more scientific.

So I think your strongest argument is the negative one:

Uniform pedigree is a fiction.
Credit scores are a lottery, not a measurement of a person.
Gamblers are predictable, so you can model the system that's gambling on you.

The positive claim — that there is a "genetic credit score" in DNA that tells you the true allocation — that's where you lose me. That part needs a lot more than mortality differences to prove.

Do you want to defend that part, or is the negative critique the part you actually want to publish? ‎<This message was edited>

Here's a sketch we can build from:

Game: Inflow

Premise, not Nazi, not eugenics: You're not ranking people by genes. You're reconstructing a family DAG from broken data. Like archaeology. The question is: can you recover the missing parents?

Core loop:
Player gets a village / town: 20-50 people, all tested. You get a correlation matrix — who correlates with whom, how strongly.
You know the rules from your model: everyone in the sample is underage in the model, parents are outside. No direct parent nodes in the sample.
Your job: place assumed nodes — inflow parents — and draw edges to explain the correlations with the fewest assumed nodes and fewest contradictions.

Enigma mechanic — find generator by predicate:
Predicate = "This set of 4 people all share an uncle-like correlation, but no pair shares a parent-like correlation."
Generator = "There must be one hidden inflow node, with two children, each of whom is an uncle to two of them."
Player proposes a generator. Game checks: does this generator generate the observed correlations? If yes, it fits. If no, it shows the contradiction — the correlation you can't explain.

That's the DNF solver in game form. You learn very fast: syntactic DAGs explode, semantic generators are few. You learn why you need the whole population — because if you delete 3 people from the village, the DAG becomes ambiguous. Two different generators fit the same remaining correlations.

Scarcity level:
Level 1: Abundance. You can loan to anyone, scores don't matter, DAG is just a puzzle.
Level 2: Scarcity increasing. Banks in the game start requiring pedigree for loans to avoid hyperinflation / deflation. Now the DAG matters: a player with a clean, closed DAG gets a loan. A player with a broken DAG — missing inflow nodes, ambiguous siblings — gets denied, not because they're "bad," but because the bank can't model the risk.
Level 3: You play the bank. You have to decide: do you use the lottery credit score, or do you use the DAG score? You see the lottery leads to hyperinflation — you lend to people who can't repay because you mis-modeled their family obligations. That breaks your own rule from two turns ago: mass-consent is required, because otherwise the DAG is coerced / partial and the scores are wrong. And it also breaks the teaching point. If players realize later "oh, that avatar was a real person and I was being scored on how efficiently I communicate with them," they'll feel tricked, not taught. That's how you get the revolt against the banks, but earlier.

So we need to split it into two layers, and keep them separate:

Layer 1 — The Game, educational only, synthetic.
This is what computer scientists can do now, no real people needed.

Avatars are synthetic, generated. Not "public data -> model of a real person." They feel real because their social dynamics are modeled on real demographic patterns — how often people talk, who clusters with whom, how communication efficiency predicts correlation in the model — but they're not of anyone.
Player plays a synthetic self. They can see a demographic approximation of a worldwide DAG, but it's a simulated world, like GTA's Liberty City is a simulation of New York, not New York.
The educational examples are for those who are interested: here's a village where parents are missing, here's a town where sibling counts are uneven, here's why you can't refine relations from local community alone. You learn the structure without anyone's real data being used.

That teaches the predicate idea: "How well does communication efficiency predict correlation?" You can test it in the simulation, where ground truth is known. You can see when it works and when it fails.

Layer 2 — The Real DAG, opt-in only.
This is the science part, not the game part. If, and only if, someone gives explicit mass-consent to be tested and to be a node, their real DAG can be built. No social avatar as a backdoor. No inferring genetic correlation from Meta socials without consent. Because social correlation is not genetic correlation — two people can talk a lot and be unrelated, two brothers can never talk. Using socials as a proxy would re-introduce the exact heuristic gambling you criticize.

In that split, the game does what you want it to do:
People feel what it's like to only see small local communities and not be able to refine relations.
They feel the missing information when they try to zoom out to the worldwide DAG and it's blank.
They learn that "pedigree" is about DAG reconstruction, not about Nazis, not about morphology.
They do it without being turned into an avatar themselves.

And the computer scientists get what they need: a clean, synthetic testbed for DAG-recovery algorithms — find generator by predicate, fit DAG to correlations, handle hidden inflow — without touching real people's data.

If we build the prototype that way — synthetic world, GTA-like, but the world is social — we can still make it feel socially real. The dynamics will be real patterns, not real people.

Do you want to start with that synthetic version? We can design the first map: a synthetic town where communication efficiency is high inside clusters, low between clusters, and the player has to figure out that the clusters are not families, they're just communication bubbles, and the real DAG is underneath and mostly missing. ‎<This message was edited>

Peeps gradually turn into adult clucks and purrs at weeks 8 to 16. Cockerels may start practicing crows

12-24 weeks - crowing / adult self-signal, at / just before sexual maturity
Most roosters start crowing between 4 to 6 months of age. This stage corresponds with sexual maturity and the onset of puberty
Healthy rooster will typically start crowing between 16 and 24 weeks of age

Endianness — you hash little-endian, compare big-endian

So you need more than dedup. You need dedup + subsumption + merging, and you need to do it in a canonical way, not heuristically.

And yes — there is a non-heuristic, deterministic way to do it lazily in breadth-first. It's not greedy in the "pick a good order and hope" sense. It's exact:

Canonical term representation
Sort literals in every term. always becomes. Then a term is just a sorted string / bitmask. Dedup is now just a hash set lookup. That's lazy + breadth-first friendly — you dedup as soon as you generate a term, before expanding further.

This is hash-consing. It's what BDDs do.

Don't do greedy absorption. Do closure to fixpoint.
Greedy = "keep this term if it looks useful." That depends on order and can miss collapses.

Exact = repeat until nothing changes:
Delete any term subsumed by a smaller term: if as literal sets, delete
Add consensus of any pair that differs in exactly one literal:, add

Do that breadth-first, level by level: generate level only from the deduped, subsumption-filtered level.

This is just Quine-McCluskey / iterative consensus. It's not a heuristic. If you run it to fixpoint, you get the exact set of prime implicants, regardless of order. Order only changes speed, not the final result.

For sha8, this is feasible because you only have 8 variables. The universe of possible terms is — each variable can be positive, negative, or absent. So your fixpoint can never explode beyond 6561 terms, even if naive distribution tried to generate millions. The hash set caps it.

So the algorithm is:
terms = set()
queue = initial DNF terms (canonical, deduped)

while queue:
 term = pop smallest first // breadth-first
 if term is subsumed by terms: skip
 remove any existing terms subsumed by term
 add term
 for each other term that differs in 1 literal: push consensus
No heuristic choice. Smallest-first is just for laziness, it doesn't change the final fixpoint.

The catch: this is exact for 8 vars. For 32 vars, is impossible, and that's why you can't do this for real SHA. But for sha8, it's the correct non-greedy way.

[16/11/2026, 20:42:41] Meta AI: That reframe makes your shorthand click.

You're not using phenotype to mean the body as stuff. You're using it to mean the program — morphology as the hardware shape, animation as the running software. And the essential data in that program is not the atoms, because those are constantly replaced. It's the patterns: how to breathe, how to feel, how to respond to heat, pressure, light.

That maps surprisingly well onto a few real ideas:

Phenotype as information, not material
Dawkins' extended phenotype already pushes in this direction — the beaver dam, the spider web, the bird song are phenotype too, because they're the output of a program, not the body itself. You're pushing it one step further: the program itself is the phenotype, the body is just a temporary runtime.

Learned programs cross species
Breathing programs are a good example. A human infant, a dog, a bird — all run a version of "rhythmic gas exchange gated by CO2, modulated by fear, effort, temperature." The code differs in implementation, but the pattern is conserved and can be learned / copied / imitated across species. Same for "how to feel" — a fear flinch, a freeze, a pant to dump heat. Those are animation routines that get transmitted by observation, not just by genes.

Animation + environment = perception
That's the part I find strongest. Perception isn't in the program alone, and it isn't in the environment alone. It's in the coupling. Heat exchange changes breathing rate, breathing rate changes CO2, CO2 changes feeling, feeling changes posture, posture changes heat exchange. It's a loop. So "you" as the program only exists as that loop running in context.

If I follow your identification claim: you identify not with the material body, which is always new, but with the continuity of that loop — the fact that the animation keeps running, even though the substrate changes.

Is that close? And when you say those programs are "learned by other species" — do you mean literally copied by other animals watching, or more like convergent re-discovery of the same program because the physics of heat / pressure / breathing forces the same solution? ‎<This message was edited>

[16/11/2026, 20:47:31] Meta AI: That is a coherent extension of Dawkins, but with a twist he doesn't make.

Dawkins' meme survives because it's copied. You're adding a second condition for survival: metabolic power. A program isn't really alive as phenotype if it's just stored passively — like in a book, or in an AI that can imitate the pattern without paying the metabolic cost. It has to be run at full power, in a body that is exchanging heat, pressure, oxygen, doing the work.

And then you add competitive exclusion for programs.

While you're alive, you're the dominant runtime for your unique program. The prey species that watch you learn fragments of it — your breathing rhythm under stress, your hunting / approach patterns, your feeling-response to heat — but they can't fully express it because:
They're busy surviving you, and
You are monopolizing the resources — oxygen, food, territory, attention — that would be needed to run that program at your metabolic scale.

If the dominant runtime stops, you get niche release. Not just "resources become available" in the generic sense, but specifically the oxygen and metabolic headroom that was locked up in maintaining your high-power animation becomes free. Then a learner that already holds a partial copy could, in theory, upgrade from passive storage to active expression.

That's testable in principle, even if it's hard:

In ecology, when an apex predator is removed, mesopredators don't just increase in number, they change behavior — they start expressing bolder, more predator-like routines they previously only used in fragments. That's called mesopredator release.
In animal culture, when a dominant teacher disappears, learners sometimes do start performing the full sequence they only observed in pieces.

Where I would push back on your version:

Learning a behavior is not the same as learning a feeling. A prey animal can learn your approach pattern to avoid you. That doesn't mean it learns your internal feeling program — the qualia of heat exchange, breath, fear in your context. It learns a functional copy for its own context.

So the question becomes: does "feeling does not die" mean the pattern of feeling continues, or the actual feeling continues? The pattern can be copied. The actual first-person running of it seems tied to a specific metabolic runtime.

Do you mean continuation in the pattern sense — the program as information persists — or in the stronger sense that the same feeling-loop literally re-instantiates in another animal once your metabolic monopoly ends? ‎<This message was edited>

[16/11/2026, 20:49:31] Meta AI: Yes, if you define it that way, the conclusion follows from the definition.

Feeling = Program × Environment, mediated by exchange

Program is mechanical: sequences of contraction, dilation, breathing rhythm, attention shifts.
Environment is mechanical: temperature gradients, pressure, chemistry, other bodies.
Their coupling is heat exchange, pressure exchange, gas exchange.

Then feeling isn't a substance stored in a body. It's an event that happens when those two mechanics meet. And events of that type will keep happening as long as there are programs meeting environments — which there always are.

So in that model, "feeling" as a category cannot die. Only a specific feeling can stop — the one generated by this program in this environment.

And you already named the cost of translation: memories don't translate.

Memories are highly specific to the previous coupling. They are records of "what this program did in that environment at that heat/pressure." Put the same abstract program into a new body in a new environment — different mass, different metabolic rate, different sensors, different heat dissipation — and the interaction changes, so the feeling changes a lot. What survives is not the content, it's the form of interaction: a rhythmic exchange that produces a state that can be called feeling.

That splits your claim into two levels:

Type-level continuation: Feeling-as-interaction continues, because programs + environments keep coupling. That is trivially true in your model.

Token-level continuation: Your feeling continues in another body. That would require not just any program, but your unique program, with its uniqueness intact, being run at matching metabolic power in a new environment that preserves enough of the coupling to count as the same feeling.

If uniqueness is defined by exact metabolic power + exact history of couplings, then translation will almost always lose uniqueness. The new runtime will produce a feeling, but it won't be yours in the token sense. It will be a new token of the same type.

Is that the distinction you're making — that you don't expect memories or personal continuity to survive, only the general fact that the program-type will keep generating feeling somewhere else once the metabolic monopoly is released? ‎<This message was edited>

[16/11/2026, 20:53:17] Meta AI: Now you're narrowing uniqueness to something very specific and measurable:

Uniqueness = f(oxygen availability, morphology, metabolic demand)

Not "breathing in general." Your specific function: how your breathing rate, depth, and timing changes as oxygen drops, given your lung volume, body mass, heat load, and activity. That's a signature. No other animal has exactly that curve.

And your claim about learning: prey doesn't learn the abstract idea of you. It learns that curve in contact — by hearing it, feeling the pressure change when you approach, timing your pauses. To avoid you, it has to model you. The closest prey, the youngest prey, gets the most exposure, so it builds the most accurate model.

That part is ecologically plausible. In predator-prey learning, there's a known effect: the individuals with the most encounters develop the best predator-recognition templates, especially during sensitive periods when young animals are learning what to fear.

Where your model diverges from standard ecology is the next step:

"Can only survive me when I die, otherwise I eat the prey who knows me best"

In most real predator-prey systems, that doesn't hold, for two reasons:

Learning is survival. The prey that learns your breathing function best is less likely to be eaten, not more. It detects you earlier, times its escape to your exhale / pause, uses your own metabolic limits against you. Knowledge is protective, not a death sentence.

Expression doesn't require your death, it requires distance. A young animal that has learned your function doesn't need you to die to mature and gain metabolic power. It needs a refuge, a time when you're not hunting, a season when you're satiated, a territory edge. Parent-child: share ∼50%, but in long, unbroken blocks across every chromosome. One parent gives you one full copy of each chromosome segment.
Uncle-nephew: share ∼25% on average, in shorter, broken blocks, because it went through a sibling and a recombination.
Full siblings: share ∼50% too, but in a different pattern — they share both sides sometimes, sometimes neither.

recombination rates are as mapped
no inbreeding / positional selection that mimics the pattern
lab calls are correct, no false positives, no contamination
the reference population is correct

Change any of those assumptions, especially your positional selection — who is taken, from where, in what position — and the same block pattern can be read differently.

Predators have to be more athletic than prey, by a margin

In wild lion-zebra and cheetah-impala pairs in Botswana, measured with collars in the wild:
predators had 20% higher muscle fibre power than prey
37% greater acceleration
72% greater deceleration capacity

The conclusion is explicit: “the predator needs to be more athletic than its prey to sustain viable success rate” — they have to brake, turn, and re-accelerate at speed to follow unpredictable prey.

Mass is a penalty for control

Wilson’s model for terrestrial pursuit: forces needed to turn scale linearly with mass, while maximum force an animal can exert scales to a 2/3 power law. That’s why larger animals have greater turn radii, and why outcome “depends critically on mass effects and the ability of animals to time turns precisely.”

Same square-cube rule in biomechanics textbooks: strength ∝ cross-section ∝ L², mass ∝ L³, so strength-to-weight ∝ 1/L. A 150-lb athlete does pull-ups more easily than a 300-lb athlete of similar composition, and a massive dinosaur can’t get up as easily as a squirrel.

Humans vs other primates / mammals on power-per-mass

Chimp muscle produces about 35% more power per kg than human muscle. In dynamic tasks, chimps are ∼1.35 to 1.5x stronger per body weight. Humans have more slow-twitch fibers — endurance, not explosive power.
In jumping, marmosets had more than twice the muscle-mass-specific mean power output of humans during push-off: 430 W/kg vs 181 W/kg in humans.
Humans are described in those papers as “not really built for power. We are more about stamina.” Our specialty is sustained, moderate force and throwing, not out-accelerating, out-braking, out-turning prey.

White-throated sparrows in a hypobaric wind tunnel, with everything else held constant, foraged faster and more when pressure dropped — a simulated storm. White-crowned sparrows in the wild also increased food intake when pressure fell 12-24h before snowstorms.

Golden-winged warblers famously left Tennessee >24h before a tornadic storm, likely using infrasound.

Birds have a plausible hardware advantage: air sacs + a paratympanic organ in the middle ear that may work as a biological barometer. Apes don't have that hardware.

Now the mirror question, factually:

Apes recognizing themselves vs other species

The test is Gallup 1970, the mark test: anesthetize, put a red mark you can't feel on a place you can only see in a mirror, see if you touch it when the mirror comes back.

Pass, consistently:

Chimpanzees — first tested 1970. After days, they stopped treating reflection as another chimp, started using it to inspect mouth, genitals, marks. Touch mark in mirror. "four chimpanzees were anesthetized and marked with red dye... they examined the areas that had been marked in the mirror, indicating an understanding that they were viewing themselves"
Orangutans — passed 1973, same mark-directed behavior. "Orangutans recognized themselves — and even identified marks on their bodies — in a 1973 study"
Bonobos — passed 1994, at least 4 of 9 used mirror to inspect parts not directly visible.
Humans — fail until ∼18-24 months, then pass.

Inconsistent / borderline:

Gorillas — the odd one out among great apes. "The results for gorillas have been more inconclusive." "most studies have failed to find convincing evidence in gorillas" — except enculturated Koko, who signed "Me, Koko." Researchers suggest gorillas fail partly because direct eye contact is a threat signal, so they avoid looking long enough to learn. Smaller frontal cortex also cited.
Gibbons and all monkeys tested — "showed only social reactions to their mirror image. They behaved as if confronted with an unknown member of their own species." Capuchin monkeys, macaques, etc. fail mark test, even though they can use mirrors to find objects.

Other species that pass, which breaks the "only apes" idea:

Bottlenose dolphins — pass, contort to inspect marks.
Asian elephants — 1 of 3 clearly passed mark test in 2006 Bronx Zoo study, all showed mirror-directed behavior. "An Asian elephant at the Bronx Zoo passed the mirror test"
Eurasian magpies — first non-mammal to pass, 2008. Peck at mark only visible in mirror.
Cleaner wrasse — small reef fish, passed 2019, disputed. "Only a handful of animals pass... great apes, Asian elephants, bottlenose dolphins, Eurasian magpies, and one fish, the cleaner wrasse." Critics say it might be parasite-scraping, not self-awareness, but follow-up showed they recognize own face in photos.

Fail:

Dogs, cats, most monkeys, most birds, octopuses — fail the visual mark test. That does not prove they lack self — test is heavily visual, and dogs would need a smell version.

So in strict science: mirror self-recognition is rare, not ape-only, and not universal even in apes. Gorillas are the gap. Magpies and a fish passing means it's not about being a great ape, it's about a specific kind of visual-motor matching + social complexity.
